@runtime_checkable
class ParserBackend(Protocol):  # pylint: disable=too-few-public-methods
    """Protocol defining the interface for parser backends.

    All parser backends must implement this protocol to be usable with headerkit.
    Backends are responsible for translating from their native AST format
    (pycparser, libclang, etc.) to the common :class:`Header` IR format.

    Available Backends
    ------------------
    * ``libclang`` - LLVM clang-based parser with C++ support

    Example
    -------
    ::

        from headerkit.backends import get_backend

        # Get default backend
        backend = get_backend()

        # Get specific backend
        libclang = get_backend("libclang")

        # Parse code
        header = backend.parse("int foo(void);", "test.h")
    """

    # pylint: disable=unnecessary-ellipsis

    def parse(
        self,
        code: str,
        filename: str,
        include_dirs: list[str] | None = None,
        extra_args: list[str] | None = None,
        *,
        use_default_includes: bool = True,
        recursive_includes: bool = True,
        max_depth: int = 10,
        project_prefixes: tuple[str, ...] | None = None,
        allowlist: list[str] | None = None,
        denylist: list[str] | None = None,
    ) -> Header:
        """Parse C/C++ code and return the IR representation.

        Traversal and filtering
        -----------------------
        ``recursive_includes`` governs *traversal*: descending into each
        non-system included header and merging what it declares.
        ``project_prefixes`` decides which paths count as project rather than
        system headers, and ``max_depth`` (with a backend-internal cycle guard)
        bounds the descent.

        ``allowlist`` and ``denylist`` govern *filtering*, and they narrow the
        merged result in **both** traversal modes:

        * ``recursive_includes=True`` with no ``allowlist`` returns declarations
          from every non-system included header.
        * ``recursive_includes=True`` with an ``allowlist`` returns the main
          file's declarations plus those of the named files, and nothing else.
        * ``recursive_includes=False`` with no ``allowlist`` returns the main
          file's declarations alone.
        * **Deny wins over allow.** A file named by both lists is excluded.
        * The main file is never denied; a denylist governs included files only.
        * A list entry matching nothing is not an error.

        :param code: Source code to parse.
        :param filename: Name of the source file. Used for error messages
            and ``#line`` directives. Does not need to exist on disk.
        :param include_dirs: Directories to search for ``#include`` files.
            Only used by backends that handle preprocessing.
        :param extra_args: Additional arguments for the preprocessor/compiler.
            Format is backend-specific.
        :param use_default_includes: If True, add system include directories.
        :param recursive_includes: If True, descend into included project headers
            and merge their declarations into the result. False parses only the
            main file, and is the only way to exclude included declarations
            entirely.
        :param max_depth: Maximum recursion depth for include processing.
        :param project_prefixes: Path prefixes to treat as project headers rather
            than system headers, so that they are descended into.
        :param allowlist: Files whose declarations are kept, alongside the main
            file's own. ``None`` keeps every non-system file reached by traversal.
            Absolute entries are used as-is; relative entries (including a bare
            basename) resolve against the parsed file's directory, then
            ``include_dirs``, then the current working directory. An entry
            containing ``*``, ``?`` or ``[`` is an :mod:`fnmatch` pattern whose
            directory part resolves the same way. Matching is on whole resolved
            paths, never substrings.
        :param denylist: Files whose declarations are dropped, using the same
            resolution and glob rules as ``allowlist``. Deny wins over allow. A
            denylist with no allowlist means "everything except these". The
            parsed file itself cannot be denied.
        :returns: Parsed header containing all extracted declarations.
        :raises RuntimeError: If parsing fails due to syntax errors.
        """
        ...

    @property
    def name(self) -> str:
        """Human-readable name of this backend (e.g., ``"pycparser"``)."""
        ...

    @property
    def supports_macros(self) -> bool:
        """Whether this backend can extract ``#define`` constants."""
        ...

    @property
    def supports_cpp(self) -> bool:
        """Whether this backend can parse C++ code."""
        ...

    @property
    def supported_languages(self) -> frozenset[str]:
        """Set of source languages supported by this backend (e.g., ``frozenset({"c", "cpp"})``)."""
        ...

    @property
    def supported_classifications(self) -> frozenset[str]:
        """Set of input classifications supported by this backend (e.g., ``frozenset({"header", "source"})``)."""
        ...

docs.title: Docker Usage
docs.text:
autopxd2 provides a Docker image with libclang pre-installed, allowing you to generate high-quality .pxd files without installing clang on your system.

No local LLVM installation needed

The Docker image includes libclang pre-installed, so you don't need to install LLVM on your system.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Use the pre-built image from GitHub Container Registry:

docker pull ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2

Or build locally:

git clone https://github.com/elijahr/python-autopxd2.git
cd python-autopxd2
docker build -t ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 .

docs.title: Generate pxd from a header file
docs.text:
The container runs in /work by default, so mount your project there:

# Mount current directory to /work and generate pxd
docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work -w /work ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 \
    autopxd myheader.h

# Save output to a file
docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work -w /work ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 \
    autopxd myheader.h > myheader.pxd

docs.title: C++ headers
docs.text:
# libclang is used by default in the container
docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work -w /work ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 \
    autopxd myheader.hpp

docs.title: Include directories
docs.text:
System include paths are automatically detected inside the container. For project-specific headers, mount the directories and use -I:

# Project includes (already under /work)
docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work -w /work ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 \
    autopxd -I include -I src myheader.h

For external dependencies outside your project, mount them separately:

# Mount external library to /third_party
docker run --rm \
    -v $(pwd):/work \
    -v ~/libs/somelib:/third_party \
    -w /work \
    ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 \
    autopxd -I include -I /third_party/include myheader.h

Important: Any directory referenced with -I must be accessible inside the container. Use relative paths for directories under /work, or mount external directories and use absolute paths.

docs.title: Interactive shell
docs.text:
# Get an interactive shell in the container
docker run --rm -it -v $(pwd):/work -w /work ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 bash

# Then run autopxd commands interactively (paths are relative to /work)
autopxd -I include myheader.h

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
For projects that frequently use autopxd2, add it to your docker-compose.yml:

services:
  autopxd:
    image: ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2
    volumes:
      - .:/work
    working_dir: /work

Then run:

docker compose run --rm autopxd autopxd myheader.h

docs.title: What's Included
docs.text:
The Docker image includes:

  • Python 3.12
  • clang and libclang development libraries
  • autopxd2 with all dependencies
  • The clang Python package for libclang bindings

docs.title: Building for Different Architectures
docs.text:
The Dockerfile supports both AMD64 and ARM64 architectures:

# Build for current architecture
docker build -t autopxd2 .

# Build for specific architecture
docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t autopxd2:amd64 .
docker build --platform linux/arm64 -t autopxd2:arm64 .

docs.title: Recommended Installation
docs.text:
Install autopxd2:

pip install autopxd2

autopxd2 uses headerkit, which vendors LLVM clang Python bindings for LLVM 18–23 directly. There is no need to install a separate clang2 or clang Python package.

You only need the system libclang shared library (libclang.so, libclang.dylib, or libclang.dll).

docs.title: Automatic libclang Installation
docs.text:
HeaderKit provides a built-in installer to automatically download and set up libclang for your platform:

python -m headerkit.install_libclang

docs.title: Without LLVM: the tree-sitter Backend
docs.text:
If you cannot install a system libclang, install the treesitter extra instead:

pip install "autopxd2[treesitter]"

Then pass --backend tree-sitter:

autopxd --backend tree-sitter myheader.h myheader.pxd

This backend parses only the file you give it: it does not follow #include directives, does not extract #define macros, does not detect system include paths, and rejects --std and --clang-arg. See Parser Backends.

docs.title: System Package Managers
docs.text: Alternatively, you can install LLVM / libclang using your system's package manager:

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: brew install llvm

docs.title: Ubuntu / Debian
docs.text: sudo apt-get install libclang-dev llvm

docs.title: Alpine Linux / musl
docs.text: apk add clang-dev

docs.title: Fedora / RHEL
docs.text: sudo dnf install clang-devel llvm

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
1. Install LLVM from releases.llvm.org or via winget install LLVM.LLVM
  2. Ensure the LLVM bin directory is in your PATH

docs.title: Headless CI & Build Containers (cibuildwheel, Docker)
docs.text:
In minimal Docker containers or CI build environments (such as Alpine/musllinux, manylinux, or slim Debian images) where libclang is not present, you can:

  1. Install libclang in the container:
  2. Alpine / musllinux: apk add clang-dev
  3. Debian / Ubuntu: apt-get install -y libclang-dev
  4. RHEL / manylinux: dnf install -y clang-devel

(For example, in cibuildwheel config in pyproject.toml:) 

[[tool.cibuildwheel.overrides]]
select = ["*-musllinux_*"]
before-all = "apk add clang-dev"

  1. Or use the Tree-sitter backend (no system packages required): Declare autopxd2[treesitter] in your build dependencies: 
    [build-system]
requires = ["meson-python", "autopxd2[treesitter]"]
    and pass --backend tree-sitter in your build script (e.g. meson.build).

docs.title: Development Installation
docs.text:
For development, clone the repository and install with development dependencies:

git clone https://github.com/elijahr/python-autopxd2.git
cd python-autopxd2
pip install -e .[dev]

docs.title: Docker (No Installation Required)
docs.text:
Use the Docker image for pre-configured libclang support without installing anything on your host system:

docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work -w /work ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 autopxd myheader.h

See Docker Usage for more details.

docs.title: Verifying Installation
docs.text:
Check that autopxd2 can find libclang:

autopxd --list-backends

If libclang is installed correctly, you will see:

Available backends:
  libclang     Full C/C++ support via LLVM [available] (default)
  tree-sitter  Fast C/C++ parsing without system LLVM dependencies [available]

Default: libclang

The tree-sitter line appears once the treesitter extra is installed; it is listed as unavailable otherwise.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This guide will get you generating Cython .pxd files in under 5 minutes.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Given a C header file example.h:

// example.h
typedef struct {
    int x;
    int y;
} Point;

Point create_point(int x, int y);
double distance(Point a, Point b);

Generate a .pxd file:

autopxd example.h > example.pxd

This produces:

cdef extern from "example.h":

    cdef struct Point:
        int x
        int y

    Point create_point(int x, int y)

    double distance(Point a, Point b)

docs.title: Include Directories
docs.text:
The libclang backend automatically detects system include paths, so standard headers like <stddef.h> and <stdint.h> work out of the box.

For project-specific includes, use -I:

autopxd -I ./include -I ./third_party myheader.h

To disable automatic system include detection (e.g., for cross-compilation), use --no-default-includes:

autopxd --no-default-includes -I /custom/sysroot/include myheader.h

docs.title: Using with Cython
docs.text:
After generating the .pxd file, use it in your Cython code:

# mymodule.pyx
from example cimport Point, create_point, distance

def make_point(x: int, y: int) -> tuple:
    cdef Point p = create_point(x, y)
    return (p.x, p.y)

def calc_distance(p1: tuple, p2: tuple) -> float:
    cdef Point a, b
    a.x, a.y = p1
    b.x, b.y = p2
    return distance(a, b)

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
You can also use autopxd2 programmatically:

from headerkit.backends import get_backend
from headerkit.writers.cython import write_pxd

# Parse a header file
backend = get_backend("libclang")
with open("example.h") as f:
    code = f.read()

header = backend.parse(code, "example.h")

# Generate pxd content
pxd = write_pxd(header)
print(pxd)

docs.title: Parser Backends
docs.text:
autopxd2 ships two parser backends: libclang (the default) and tree-sitter.

$ autopxd --list-backends
Available backends:
  libclang     Full C/C++ support via LLVM [available] (default)
  tree-sitter  Fast C/C++ parsing without system LLVM dependencies [available]

Default: libclang

docs.title: Choosing a Backend
docs.text:
libclang tree-sitter Install needs the system libclang shared library pip install "autopxd2[treesitter]", no system LLVM Follows #include directives ✅ ❌ (parses the given file only) #define macro extraction ✅ ❌ System include path detection ✅ ❌ C++ classes, templates, namespaces ✅ ✅ --std / --clang-arg ✅ ❌ (rejected with an error)

Use libclang unless you cannot install LLVM. Use tree-sitter for self-contained headers in environments (such as minimal CI or Docker containers) where a system libclang is unavailable.

docs.title: libclang
docs.text:
Uses LLVM's clang library for parsing. Provides the same parser used by production compilers.

Features:

  • Full C++ support (classes, templates, namespaces)
  • Extracts macros as constants (integers, floats, strings, expressions)
  • Automatic system include path detection
  • Follows and recursively expands #include directives across translation units
  • Handles comments and preprocessor directives directly
  • Better error messages
  • Handles complex and umbrella headers reliably

Limitations:

  • Requires libclang shared library to be available on your system (use python -m headerkit.install_libclang or install LLVM manually)
  • Function-like macros are not extracted

Usage:

autopxd myheader.h

# For C++ headers
autopxd myheader.hpp

docs.title: tree-sitter
docs.text:
Uses tree-sitter grammars for C and C++. It needs no system LLVM, so it installs and runs anywhere Python does using pre-built PyPI wheels.

Install:

pip install "autopxd2[treesitter]"

Usage:

autopxd --backend tree-sitter myheader.h

# C++ works too
autopxd --backend tree-sitter --cpp myclass.hpp

Limitations:

The tree-sitter backend is substantially more limited than libclang:

  • No #include recursion: It parses only the file given to it. Given #include "inner.h" or #include <header.h>, declarations from the included headers do not appear in the output; only the parsed file's own declarations do. If the header relies on types defined in included files, those type definitions will not be present.
  • No #define macro extraction: Constants and macro functions defined via #define are not extracted into the .pxd.
  • No system include paths: It does not query or search compiler system include directories.
  • Rejects compiler driver options: Options that configure the compiler frontend (--std and --clang-arg) are rejected with an explicit error:
$ autopxd --backend tree-sitter --std c11 myheader.h
Error: --std is only supported by the libclang backend, but the resolved backend is 'tree-sitter'.
Use --backend libclang, or drop the option.

When to use tree-sitter: - Single, self-contained C or C++ header files. - Headless CI pipelines, Docker containers, or minimal environments (e.g. Alpine/musllinux) where installing LLVM/Clang is impractical. - When you do not need macro constants or included header declarations in the generated .pxd.

docs.title: System Include Paths
docs.text:
The libclang backend automatically detects system include directories by querying the system clang compiler. This means headers like <stddef.h> and <stdint.h> work without requiring manual -I flags.

# This works automatically - system includes are detected
autopxd myheader.h

To disable automatic include detection:

autopxd --no-default-includes myheader.h

You can still add additional include directories:

autopxd -I /my/project/include myheader.h

docs.title: Macro Extraction
docs.text: The libclang backend extracts #define macros as Cython constant declarations. The type is automatically detected from the macro value.

docs.title: Integer Macros
docs.text:
#define SIZE 100
#define MASK 0xFF
#define MODE 0755
#define FLAGS 0b1010
#define BIG_NUM 100ULL

Generates int declarations:

    int SIZE
    int MASK
    int MODE
    int FLAGS
    int BIG_NUM

Supported formats: decimal, hex (0x), octal (0), binary (0b), with optional type suffixes (U, L, UL, LL, ULL).

docs.title: Floating-Point Macros
docs.text:
#define PI 3.14159
#define EPSILON 1e-10
#define FACTOR 2.5f

Generates double declarations:

    double PI
    double EPSILON
    double FACTOR

docs.title: String Macros
docs.text:
#define VERSION "1.0.0"
#define APP_NAME "myapp"

Generates const char* declarations:

    const char* VERSION
    const char* APP_NAME

docs.title: Expression Macros
docs.text:
#define A 10
#define B 20
#define TOTAL (A + B)
#define FLAGS (0x01 | 0x02)
#define NEGATIVE -1

Expression macros that consist of numeric literals, operators, and other macro references are detected and declared with appropriate types:

    int A
    int B
    int TOTAL
    int FLAGS
    int NEGATIVE

docs.title: Unsupported Macros (silently ignored)
docs.text:
• Function-like macros: #define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))
  • Empty macros: #define EMPTY
  • String concatenation: #define CONCAT "hello" "world"

docs.title: C++ Template Support
docs.text: The backends support C++ templates, including primary templates and full specializations.

docs.title: Primary Templates
docs.text:
C++ class templates with type parameters are translated to Cython's template syntax:

template<typename T>
class Container {
public:
    T value;
    T get();
    void set(T v);
};

Generates:

cdef cppclass Container[T]:
    T value
    T get()
    void set(T v)

Multiple type parameters are supported:

template<typename K, typename V>
class Map {
public:
    V lookup(K key);
    void insert(K key, V value);
};

Generates:

cdef cppclass Map[K, V]:
    V lookup(K key)
    void insert(K key, V value)

docs.title: Template Specializations
docs.text:
Full template specializations are emitted with mangled Python-safe names and the original C++ name as a string literal:

template<>
class Container<int> {
public:
    int special_value;
    int get_special();
};

Generates:

cdef cppclass Container_int "Container<int>":
    int special_value
    int get_special()

The mangling scheme converts special characters to valid Python identifiers: - < and > are removed, contents become underscore-separated - * becomes _ptr - & becomes _ref - :: becomes _

Examples: - Container<int> -> Container_int - Map<int, double> -> Map_int_double - Foo<int*> -> Foo_int_ptr

docs.title: Using Docker for libclang
docs.text:
If you don't want to install libclang locally, use the Docker image:

docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work -w /work ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 autopxd myheader.h

See Docker Usage for details.

docs.title: Programmatic Backend Selection
docs.text:
from headerkit.backends import get_backend, list_backends

# List registered backends
print(list_backends())  # ['libclang', 'tree-sitter']

# Get a specific backend
backend = get_backend("libclang")

# Parse a header
header = backend.parse(code, "myheader.h")

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: The autopxd command-line tool generates Cython .pxd files from C/C++ headers.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text: autopxd [OPTIONS] [INFILE] [OUTFILE]

docs.title: -v, --version
docs.text:
Print program version and exit.

autopxd --version

docs.title: -b, --backend <name>
docs.text:
Select the parser backend. Options: auto (default), libclang, tree-sitter.

  • auto: Use the default backend (libclang) when it is available, otherwise the first available backend
  • libclang: Full C/C++ support via LLVM
  • tree-sitter: Fast C/C++ parsing without system LLVM dependencies (requires pip install "autopxd2[treesitter]")
autopxd --backend libclang myheader.hpp
autopxd --backend tree-sitter myheader.hpp

See Parser Backends for the differences between them.

docs.title: --list-backends
docs.text:
Show available backends and exit.

autopxd --list-backends

$ autopxd --list-backends
Available backends:
  libclang     Full C/C++ support via LLVM [available] (default)
  tree-sitter  Fast C/C++ parsing without system LLVM dependencies [available]

Default: libclang

docs.title: --json
docs.text:
Output in JSON format (for use with --list-backends).

autopxd --list-backends --json

docs.title: -x, --cpp
docs.text:
Parse as C++ (requires libclang backend).

autopxd --cpp myclass.hpp

docs.title: --std <standard>
docs.text:
Specify the language standard (requires libclang backend).

autopxd --std c11 myheader.h
autopxd --std c++17 myclass.hpp

docs.title: -I, --include-dir <dir>
docs.text:
Add a directory to the include search path. Can be specified multiple times.

Note: The libclang backend automatically detects system include paths (e.g., /usr/include), so you typically only need -I for project-specific directories.

autopxd -I ./include -I ./third_party myheader.h

docs.title: -D, --define <macro>
docs.text:
Define a preprocessor macro. Can be specified multiple times.

autopxd -D DEBUG -D VERSION=2 myheader.h

docs.title: --allowlist <pattern>
docs.text:
Only generate declarations from files matching the pattern. Can be specified multiple times.

A pattern with no path separator is matched against each file's basename, so types.h and *.h work wherever the file lives. A pattern with a separator is matched against the full path; a relative one is resolved against the input header's own directory, then each -I directory, then the working directory. Glob metacharacters (*, ?, [) are supported.

The allowlist applies to the input header itself as well as to everything it includes, so an allowlist that does not name the input header drops that header's declarations too.

autopxd --allowlist main.h --allowlist types.h combined.h
autopxd --allowlist 'include/*.h' combined.h

docs.title: --denylist <pattern>
docs.text:
Never generate declarations from files matching the pattern. Can be specified multiple times. Same pattern syntax as --allowlist.

Deny wins over allow. A file matching both lists is excluded. This makes "everything under include/, except the private headers" expressible directly:

autopxd --allowlist 'include/*.h' --denylist 'include/*_internal.h' combined.h

--denylist deliberately has no short flag, so -w stays unambiguous while --whitelist is being retired.

docs.title: -w, --whitelist <pattern> (deprecated)
docs.text:
Deprecated alias for --allowlist, retained with its -w short flag. It still works and behaves identically, but emits a DeprecationWarning naming --allowlist as the replacement. Use -q / --quiet to silence that warning.

Passing both --allowlist and --whitelist is an error rather than a silent precedence guess.

docs.title: Which headers contribute declarations
docs.text:
With recursion on — the default — declarations from every non-system included header are emitted, not just those of the input header. --no-recursive confines the output to the input header's own declarations.

An allowlist narrows that set in both recursion modes. Combined:

Options Declarations emitted (default) The input header, plus every non-system header it includes --no-recursive The input header only --allowlist P Of the above set, only files matching P --denylist P Of the above set, minus files matching P --allowlist P --denylist Q Files matching P and not matching Q

docs.title: --clang-arg <arg> [libclang]
docs.text:
Pass an argument directly to libclang. Can be specified multiple times.

autopxd --clang-arg -DFOO --clang-arg -I/custom/include myheader.h

docs.title: --no-default-includes [libclang]
docs.text:
Disable automatic detection of system include directories. By default, the libclang backend queries the system clang compiler to find standard include paths. Use this option if you need full control over include paths.

# Disable auto-detection and specify all paths manually
autopxd --no-default-includes -I /my/custom/sysroot/include myheader.h

docs.title: -P, --project-prefix <path> [libclang]
docs.text:
Treat headers under the specified path as project headers rather than system headers. This is essential for umbrella headers—headers that include many sub-headers but have few declarations of their own (like sodium.h, openssl/ssl.h).

Without this option, declarations from sub-headers in system locations (e.g., /usr/include, /opt/homebrew/include) are filtered out. The --project-prefix option marks paths as project headers so their declarations are included.

Can be specified multiple times for multiple prefixes.

# Include declarations from all sodium/*.h sub-headers
autopxd -I /opt/homebrew/include \
    --project-prefix /opt/homebrew/include/sodium \
    /opt/homebrew/include/sodium.h

# Multiple prefixes
autopxd -I /usr/include \
    -P /usr/include/openssl \
    -P /usr/include/crypto \
    /usr/include/openssl/ssl.h

docs.title: --no-recursive [libclang]
docs.text:
Confine the output to the input header's own declarations. By default autopxd parses every non-system header the input includes and emits their declarations too.

Recursion is controlled by this flag alone. There is no include-count or declaration-count heuristic: a header with a single include is expanded exactly like one with fifty. To keep recursion on but restrict which of the reached headers contribute, use --allowlist or --denylist instead.

autopxd --no-recursive -P /opt/homebrew/include/sodium \
    /opt/homebrew/include/sodium.h

docs.title: --max-depth <n> [libclang]
docs.text:
Limit recursion depth for umbrella header processing (default: 10). 0 disables umbrella expansion entirely, equivalent to --no-recursive.

Values of 1 or greater currently all behave the same: each included header is parsed as its own translation unit, so the compiler has already flattened that header's own includes before the recursion descends a level. Circular includes are prevented by tracking visited files, not by this limit.

Only the libclang backend follows #include directives. Passing this option to another backend emits a warning, since it cannot be honored.

autopxd --max-depth 0 -P /opt/homebrew/include/sodium \
    /opt/homebrew/include/sodium.h

docs.title: -q, --quiet
docs.text:
Suppress warnings.

autopxd -q myheader.h

docs.title: --debug / --no-debug
docs.text:
Dump preprocessor output to stderr for debugging.

autopxd --debug myheader.h 2>preprocessed.txt

docs.title: -h, --help
docs.text:
Show help message and exit.

autopxd --help

docs.title: Generate pxd from a header
docs.text: autopxd myheader.h myheader.pxd

docs.title: With include directories
docs.text: autopxd -I /opt/local/include -I ./third_party mylib.h mylib.pxd

docs.title: Using libclang for C++
docs.text: autopxd --backend libclang --cpp myclass.hpp myclass.pxd

docs.title: Using C++17 standard
docs.text: autopxd -x --std c++17 modern.hpp modern.pxd

docs.title: Working with umbrella headers
docs.text:
Umbrella headers like sodium.h include many sub-headers but define few declarations themselves. Use --project-prefix to include declarations from sub-headers:

# Generate bindings for libsodium (installed via homebrew)
autopxd -I /opt/homebrew/include \
    -P /opt/homebrew/include/sodium \
    /opt/homebrew/include/sodium.h sodium.pxd

# Generate bindings for OpenSSL
autopxd -I /usr/include \
    -P /usr/include/openssl \
    /usr/include/openssl/ssl.h ssl.pxd

docs.title: Check available backends
docs.text: autopxd --list-backends

docs.title: libclang not available
docs.text:
If you see "libclang backend not available", install libclang:

Using headerkit: 

python -m headerkit.install_libclang

Ubuntu/Debian: 

apt install libclang-dev

macOS: 

brew install llvm

Or use Docker: 

docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work -w /work ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 autopxd myheader.h

docs.title: C++ parsing fails
docs.text:
Make sure you're using the libclang backend:

autopxd --backend libclang --cpp myheader.hpp

docs.title: Empty output from umbrella headers
docs.text:
If you're parsing an umbrella header (like sodium.h) and getting empty or minimal output, the sub-headers are probably in a system location. Use --project-prefix to mark them as project headers:

# Find where the library headers are installed
pkg-config --cflags libsodium
# Output: -I/opt/homebrew/include

# Use --project-prefix with the sub-header directory
autopxd -I /opt/homebrew/include \
    -P /opt/homebrew/include/sodium \
    /opt/homebrew/include/sodium.h

You can verify the prefix is working by using --debug to see which declarations are being found.

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Parse error or invalid input 2 Invalid command-line arguments

docs.title: C++ Support
docs.text:
autopxd2 supports C++ headers through either parser backend.

Note

The libclang backend (the default) and the tree-sitter backend both parse C++. See Parser Backends for the trade-offs.

docs.title: Basic C++ Usage
docs.text:
# C++ mode is auto-detected from .hpp/.hh/.hxx extensions
autopxd --cpp myclass.hpp > myclass.pxd

Or with Docker:

docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/work -w /work ghcr.io/elijahr/python-autopxd2 autopxd myclass.hpp

docs.title: Classes & Structs
docs.text:
C++ classes and structs are converted to Cython cppclass definitions with support for multiple inheritance, constructors, @staticmethod, and const member methods.

Destructors are not emitted: a Cython cppclass block does not declare them, and Cython calls the C++ destructor automatically for stack-allocated instances.

// widget.hpp
class BaseWidget {
public:
    virtual void show();
};

class Widget : public BaseWidget {
public:
    int width;
    int height;
    Widget();
    Widget(int w, int h);
    virtual ~Widget();
    int area() const;
    static Widget create();
};

Generates:

cdef extern from "widget.hpp":

    cdef cppclass BaseWidget:
        void show()

    cdef cppclass Widget(BaseWidget):
        int width
        int height
        Widget()
        Widget(int w, int h)
        int area() const
        @staticmethod
        Widget create()

docs.title: Generic Function & Method Templates
docs.text:
Generic C++ function and method templates are fully supported using Cython template brackets syntax:

template<typename T>
T max_val(T a, T b);

Generates:

T max_val[T](T a, T b)

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Global functions are converted directly:

double distance(const Point& a, const Point& b);

Generates:

double distance(const Point& a, const Point& b)

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
Declarations inside a namespace are emitted in a dedicated cdef extern from ... namespace block:

// ns.hpp
namespace outer {
    class Widget {
    public:
        Widget();
        int value() const;
    };
    int helper(int x);
}

Generates:

cdef extern from "ns.hpp" namespace "outer":

    cdef cppclass Widget:
        Widget()
        int value() const

    int helper(int x)

Nested namespaces are joined with :::

namespace outer { namespace inner { int f(int); } }

Generates:

cdef extern from "nested.hpp" namespace "outer::inner":

    int f(int)

docs.title: Overloading
docs.text: Multiple overloaded free functions with identical names may produce conflicts in C mode. In C++ mode (--cpp), Cython natively supports function overloading.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use header-only libraries where possible for simpler integration
  2. Start with the Docker image to avoid libclang installation issues
  3. Check generated output and manually adjust for complex C++ features
  4. Consider Cython's cppclass for classes with methods you need to call

docs.title: Example Workflow
docs.text:
1. Generate initial pxd: 

    autopxd mylib.hpp > mylib.pxd

  2. Review and adjust for methods, templates, or other features

  3. Create your Cython wrapper: 

    # mylib.pyx
from mylib cimport Widget

def create_widget(width: int, height: int):
    cdef Widget w
    w.width = width
    w.height = height
    return (w.width, w.height)
